# GCMSprime

GC/MS DECONVOLUTION · QUANTIFICATION · IDENTIFICATION

Accurate integration.\
Cleaner spectra.
======================

Fast and scalable GC/MS deconvolution and quantification for single
samples or large multisample experiments to separate overlapping peaks,
with inbuilt spectral library search.

[Get started
↗](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/articles/gcms-deconvolution.md)[Search
spectral
libraries](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/articles/library-search.md)

R · Full mass spectra · CDF input · MSP & Excel output

![GCMSprime hex logo showing resolved chromatographic peaks and their
mass spectra](logo-dark.svg)

[**Deconvolve**Resolve overlapping compounds and recover their
spectra](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/articles/gcms-deconvolution.md)
[**Quantify**Integrated areas, fitted profiles and complete
reports](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/reference/gcmsDeco.md)
[**Identify**Fast spectral matching with column-specific retention
indices](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/articles/library-search.md)

A GC–MS run records mixtures of ions whenever compounds overlap in time.
GCMSprime separates these signals into elution profiles and full mass
spectra, then integrates each resolved compound. It accepts ANDI-MS CDF
files and writes an MSP library of the recovered spectra and an Excel
quantification table when requested. For a sample series, it aligns
retention times and shares spectra across related occurrences.

An alkane ladder can calibrate peak shapes and retention indices.
Supplying a spectral library adds ranked candidate matches, with the
retention-index agreement and the reference source recorded alongside
each score.

See the [16-sample benchmark](#benchmarks-against-other-software) for
peak-area and spectral recovery across seven workflows.

## Installation

``` r

install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github(c(
  "tomwenseleers/L0glm/L0glm",
  "tomwenseleers/logconNMF/logconNMF",
  "tomwenseleers/GCMSprime/GCMSprime"
))
```

The R package includes the conditional Poisson and quasi-Poisson solver.
It fits the original ion counts with compiled C++ kernels and uses
OpenMP when available. Solver selection is automatic for the requested
noise model and memory settings.

## Automatic deconvolution for single samples

One call estimates the response shape, smooth background, compound
profiles, full mass spectra and integrated areas, then writes
NIST-compatible MSP and Excel reports. An alkane ladder can calibrate
the PSF and retention indices.

``` r

library(GCMSprime)
fit <- gcmsDeco("sample.cdf", "sample.msp", xlsx_file="sample.xlsx",
  alkanes_file="alkanes.cdf", precluster=32L)
plot(fit, type="lines", file="sample_traces.pdf")
plot(fit, type="heatmap", file="sample_heatmaps.pdf")
plot(fit, type="profiles", file="sample_profiles_spectra.pdf")
```

The compound table gives apex retention times, integrated areas and the
number of fitted ions. Use the trace and heatmap plots to inspect
overlapping peaks and residual structure, and use the profile and
spectrum plots to inspect individual components.

``` r

head(fit$compounds[c("compound", "retention_time", "area", "n_ions")])
fit$seconds
spectra <- coef(fit, normalize="l1")  # unit-L1 spectra, shared 0.1% ion cutoff
```

The fit allows asymmetric and broad profiles under a hard log-concavity
constraint. The rank criterion selects the component set, and final
refinement uses every original mass channel.

### Six co-eluting hydrocarbons

The bundled cuticular-hydrocarbon window illustrates recovered elution
profiles and spectra. This short-window example uses a supplied PSF
dictionary and a constant background; individual compound shapes are
then refined.

``` r

data(gcmsData1, package="logconNMF")
writeGCMSCDF(gcmsData1, "GCMS_data1.cdf")
example_fit <- gcmsDeco("GCMS_data1.cdf", "GCMS_data1.msp",
  nwindows=1L, baseline_df=1L, precluster=7L, correlation="auto", ncores=8L,
  control=list(initial_relaxed=FALSE, fusion_passes=0L),
  psf_control=list(kernel_est=logconNMF::convKernel("gaussian", 65L,
    list(sigma=9)), maxiter=0L))
```

Among six-factor solutions with chemically plausible retention times, a
sensitivity grid over PSF widths and precluster counts selected this fit
for its combination of low GIC, accurate apex times, compact profiles
and strong enrichment of the compounds’ diagnostic ions.

[![Grey ion traces, six resolved profiles and matching spectra for six
co-eluting
hydrocarbons](reference/figures/gcms-data1-decomposition.png)](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/articles/gcms-deconvolution.html#cuticular-hydrocarbons)

### Beer volatiles and a broad acid peak

A beer-headspace window contains a strongly asymmetric acid peak mixed
with narrower neighbours. Flexible log-concave profiles accommodate this
shape while the spectra use all 518 channels. The same workflow
represents the broad acid contribution as one log-concave profile among
the narrower peaks. The single-sample tutorial reports the measured
CDF-to-MSP times and fit metrics.

[![Beer chromatogram with fitted compounds and the broad acid
contribution](reference/figures/gcms-data2-traces.png)](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/articles/gcms-deconvolution.html#beer-volatiles-and-a-broad-acid-peak)

The [single-sample
tutorial](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/articles/gcms-deconvolution.md)
includes both datasets, fitted-signal heatmaps, profile/spectrum panels,
timings and downloadable MSP/PDF outputs. [GC/MS deconvolution:
mathematical
basis](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/articles/algorithm.md)
explains the progression from known PSFs to estimated and
component-specific shapes.

## Automatic deconvolution for multiple samples

Point to a directory containing sample-group folders and a `standards/`
subdirectory with alkane calibrations. Acquisition timestamps determine
run order. The simultaneous model aligns compounds and shares their
spectra while retaining sample-specific profiles, backgrounds and areas.

``` r

experiment <- gcmsDeco("chromatograms", output_dir="experiment_results",
  precluster=32L, batch=list(plots=TRUE))
experiment$samples
experiment$areas
```

Grouped PSF regressions divide the core budget between independent
samples and native threads. The scheduler estimates how many regressions
fit in available memory, including Windows commit headroom. After those
workers exit, a single process shares the original ion counts and fitted
means. OpenMP updates elution profiles across samples. It fits each
ion’s shared spectrum and sample-specific background coefficients
independently, keeping a fixed component order within each ion. The
general identity-link solver can stream original-channel blocks from
disk. \## Benchmarks against other software

The same 16 simulated chromatograms were supplied to every program. Each
contains **10,000 scans × 550 nominal mass channels** (m/z 30–579),
covering approximately 50 minutes. Together they contain **88 million
simulated ion intensities**. Each of the **1,000 distinct compounds**
occurs in eight randomly chosen samples. The design therefore contains
**8,000 positive sample–compound pairs**. Rank here counts the distinct
generating compounds across the batch, each with a time-local elution
profile in each positive sample. Of the compounds, 990 have
exponentially modified Gaussian (EMG) peaks and ten have a rising
shark-fin profile with an abrupt trailing edge. Higher concentrations
broaden both types. The acquisition clock allows a smooth retention
shift of up to 2.93 seconds between the first and last injections and
approximately 2% variation in scan spacing.

GCMSprime, using simultaneous logconNMF, **recovered the true rank of
1,000 exactly** in **35.95 seconds per sample**. It recovered **8,000 of
8,000** compound occurrences and made **no false-positive calls**. The
recovered peaks included **80 of the 80 acid occurrences**. MSHub
returned **1,414 deconvolved components**, 41.4% above the true rank.
The other five workflows produce peak lists or aligned feature groups.
Their outputs do not define a common factorisation rank.

The 1,000 shared factors matched the 1,000 generating compounds
one-to-one across all eight occurrences of each compound. This is exact
automatic recovery of the chemical component count from 550 measured ion
channels. Scan order distinguishes compounds that elute at different
times, and each compound contributes a shared spectrum wherever it
occurs.

Published rank-selection experiments put the scale in perspective.
Distributed NMF (DnMFk) recovered seven planted factors in a
one-terabyte matrix. Eswar et al. compared NMF rank selectors at true
rank 10. Fu et al. tested nonnegative tensor rank selection at true
ranks 15–40. The 1,000 compounds here are **25 times the largest
generating rank in that tensor experiment**. These studies use different
data models and assess different kinds of rank. [Chennupati et
al.](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11227-020-03181-6) · [Eswar et
al.](https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/3002147) · [Fu et
al.](https://doi.org/10.3390/e21070632)

| Workflow | Seconds/sample | Estimated rank (true 1,000) | TP | FP | FN | Acid TP / 80 |
|----|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| GCMSprime | 35.95 | **1,000 (exact)** | 8,000 | 0 | 0 | 80 / 80 |
| MS-DIAL | 16.02 | — | 7,728 | 11,685 | 272 | 73 / 80 |
| mzmine GC-EI | 6.92 | — | 4,202 | 185 | 3,798 | 29 / 80 |
| eRah | 25.94 | — | 7,172 | 5,615 | 828 | 70 / 80 |
| AMDIS | 28.99 | — | 7,878 | 9,122 | 122 | 80 / 80 |
| xcms + CAMERA | 4.22 | — | 7,261 | 890 | 739 | 31 / 80 |
| MSHub | 15.05 | 1,414 | 7,179 | 12,184 | 821 | 50 / 80 |

Among GCMSprime’s 8,000 matched occurrences, the median absolute
relative area error was **0.095%** and ordinary adjusted R² on the log₁₀
scale was **0.999982**.

[![Time per sample, sensitivity and precision for all seven
workflows](reference/figures/simulated-16-performance.png)](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/reference/figures/simulated-16-performance.png)

[![Estimated versus true total-ion areas across all seven
workflows](reference/figures/simulated-16-area-predictions.png)](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/reference/figures/simulated-16-area-predictions.png)

[![Reciprocal reference spectrum matches across the 16
chromatograms](reference/figures/simulated-16-spectral-violin.png)](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/reference/figures/simulated-16-spectral-violin.png)

[![Ion-support recovery across the seven
workflows](reference/figures/simulated-16-spectral-support.png)](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/reference/figures/simulated-16-spectral-support.png)

### Optimality gap to ground truth-initialised solution

The blind fit showed smooth, monotonic descent in GIC across eight
sweeps. Its final GIC differed by only **0.19%** from that of a fit
initialised with the true elution profiles and run for the same eight
sweeps. Both fits ended at the true rank of **1,000** with **8,000**
sample-level occurrences.

[![Original-ion GIC over eight sweeps of the blind fit on 16 full
chromatograms](reference/figures/full-benchmark-gic-gap.png)](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/reference/figures/full-benchmark-gic-gap.png)

[Block-level GIC
trace](https://github.com/tomwenseleers/GCMSprime/blob/master/GCMSbenchmark/inst/benchmarks/results/gic-trace.csv)
· [Final GIC
values](https://github.com/tomwenseleers/GCMSprime/blob/master/GCMSbenchmark/inst/benchmarks/results/gic-gap.csv).

### Elution profile recovery

The examples are the EMG compound and the acid with the greatest total
true area in their respective classes. Both were selected from the
simulation before comparing any fits. Each occurs in eight samples.
Solid curves show inferred profiles, dashed curves show the true
profiles, and the eight absent true profiles coincide at zero. Colours
order the 16 samples by true area. Heights retain original total-ion
intensity per scan. The mean cosine in each example uses all eight
positive occurrences, with a missing recovered profile scoring zero. The
all-acid tally covers all ten acids.

[![Recovered and simulated profiles for the selected EMG
compound](reference/figures/simulated-16-regular-profiles.png)](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/reference/figures/simulated-16-regular-profiles.png)

## Comparison with other software

On the same 16 files, GCMSprime recovered 8,000 true occurrences with
zero false calls. GNPS/MSHub estimated 1,414 batch components. MS-DIAL,
mzmine GC-EI, eRah, AMDIS and xcms + CAMERA returned peak lists or
aligned features. The seven-workflow benchmark gives their measured
recovery and timings. [Benchmark results and
settings](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/articles/benchmarks.html).

The following matrix and tensor models offer other ways to resolve
co-elution. The comparison describes their published formulations.

| Approach | What is shared and how peaks are represented | How the component count enters |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **GCMSprime / logconNMF** | A common spectrum across samples and one log-concave elution profile per occurrence. Width, asymmetry, area and retention time can vary by sample. | Grouped PSF regression proposes peaks. Original-ion GIC scores changes to the shared factors and their support. |
| **MCR-ALS, conventional GC–MS NMF and unimodal NMF** | Alternating regressions estimate elution profiles and spectra. Nonnegativity and unimodality can be imposed. Poisson MCR also models signal-dependent noise. [pyMCR](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.124.018) · [GC–MS NMF](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.talanta.2004.09.017) · [Unimodal NMF](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICASSP39728.2021.9414631) · [Poisson MCR](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chemolab.2016.02.006) | The cited fits use a chosen component count. Diagnostics can guide that choice. |
| **Simultaneous NMF and global parametric GC–MS analysis** | Simultaneous NMF shares a factor across data matrices. Parametric GC–MS analysis fits shared spectra with an explicit elution model such as an exponentially modified Gaussian. [Shared-factor NMF](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0048238) · [Global GC–MS analysis](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chemolab.2008.10.004) | The analyst specifies a candidate model order. |
| **PARAFAC and shifted PARAFAC** | Trilinear components share their spectrum and elution shape up to amplitude. Shifted PARAFAC also allows translations of that shape. [Shifted factor models](https://three-mode.leidenuniv.nl/pdf/h/harshmanhonglundy2003i.pdf) | Candidate ranks can be compared using diagnostics such as core consistency. [Bro and Kiers](https://doi.org/10.1002/cem.801) |
| **Classical PARAFAC2 and PARADISe** | Elution profiles can vary across samples subject to a common matrix of cross-products. PARADISe applies PARAFAC2 to chromatographic intervals. [PARAFAC2 for retention shifts](https://research.rug.nl/en/publications/parafac2-part-ii-modeling-chromatographic-data-with-retention-tim/) · [PARADISe](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chroma.2017.04.052) | Candidate ranks are fitted per interval. Automated model assessment is also available. [Johnsen et al.](https://doi.org/10.1002/cem.2575) |
| **Flexible and fully constrained PARAFAC2** | Flexible coupling relaxes the cross-product condition. AO-ADMM can retain the condition while imposing constraints on all modes, including the varying elution profiles. [Cohen and Bro](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-93764-9_9) · [Roald et al.](https://doi.org/10.1137/21M1450033) | Both formulations fit a specified number of components. |
| **Shift-invariant trilinearity and PARAFAC2×N** | Shift-invariant trilinearity uses Fourier-domain information to accommodate elution shifts. PARAFAC2×N extends drift modelling to multiple separation modes in multidimensional chromatography. [Shift-invariant trilinearity](https://doi.org/10.1002/cem.3501) · [PARAFAC2×N](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aca.2023.340909) | Each model is fitted at a chosen component count. |

### Commercial GC–MS software

AnalyzerPro exposes peak-width and detection thresholds. MassHunter
Unknowns Analysis can search multiple widths, with a trade-off between
resolving close peaks and runtime. LECO ChromaTOF Sync co-processes
Pegasus sample sets to improve spectra and align peaks. GCMSprime fits
one shared spectrum and a separate log-concave profile per occurrence,
and scores candidate splits against the original ion counts. The
commercial workflows have yet to be scored on these 16 chromatograms.
[AnalyzerPro](https://spectralworks.com/2016/07/08/using-analyzerpro-in-the-metabolomics-workflow/)
·
[MassHunter](https://www.agilent.com/cs/library/usermanuals/public/G3335-90243_Unknowns_Analysis_Familiarization-en.pdf#page=27)
· [ChromaTOF
Sync](https://www.leco.com/instrument/chromatof-sync-data-alignment/)
[Nine commercial workflows
compared](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/articles/benchmarks.html#commercial-gcms-deconvolution-software).

## Spectral library search

**Open and commercial libraries can be imported.** MoNA and Golm MSP
collections, GCMS-ID CSV predictions, and OpenChrom-exported Agilent or
Shimadzu libraries are supported. Large catalogues can remain in indexed
SQLite storage.

``` r

lib <- readMSP("library.msp", backend="sqlite", db_file="library.sqlite")
identified <- gcmsDeco("sample.cdf", "identified.msp",
  xlsx_file="identified.xlsx", alkanes_file="alkanes.cdf", library=lib,
  search=list(phase="DB5", ri_tolerance=30, n_matches=5,
              method=c("stein_scott", "hellinger")))
```

The compounds recovered from single- or multisample deconvolution can be
automatically annotated using **spectral match quality and retention
index**. Alkane-derived indices first restrict candidates to the
selected column class and tolerance; fast native search then ranks their
spectra. Multisample consensus IDs support a unique-compound list across
the experiment, with sample-specific RI evidence and full match
provenance retained.

Stein–Scott, cosine/angular, Hellinger and symmetric probability/count
comparisons are available, with optional ion-rarity weighting. Excel and
MSP reports include the ranked matches and annotations. The
[library-import
tutorial](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/articles/spectral-libraries.md)
covers formats and storage; [retention indices and library
search](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/articles/library-search.md)
shows single- and multisample identification. The [identification
theory](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/articles/identification-theory.md)
gives the formulas, calibration and comparison benchmarks.

## Selected references

- Lu et al. (2008) tested how concentration and component-width settings
  affected GC–TOF-MS deconvolution with AnalyzerPro, ChromaTOF and
  AMDIS. [Comparative
  evaluation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trac.2007.11.004)
- Camp (2019) describes how alternating regression lets analysts choose
  constraints separately for concentrations and spectra.
  [pyMCR](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.124.018)
- Lee et al. (2012) fit a common factor across multiple datasets.
  [Simultaneous NMF](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0048238)
- Johnsen et al. (2017) describe the PARADISe workflow for GC–MS. Roald
  et al. (2022) show how to constrain all modes of PARAFAC2.
  [PARADISe](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chroma.2017.04.052) ·
  [Constrained PARAFAC2](https://doi.org/10.1137/21M1450033)
- Aksenov et al. (2021) describe the GNPS/MSHub workflow evaluated on
  these 16 chromatograms.
  [MSHub](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41587-020-0700-3)
- Chennupati et al. (2020) infer the number of factors in large
  matrices. Fu, Matsushima and Yamanishi (2019) compare rank-selection
  criteria for nonnegative tensors. [Distributed
  NMF](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11227-020-03181-6) · [Tensor rank
  selection](https://doi.org/10.3390/e21070632)

An article describing the methods implemented in GCMSprime is in
preparation. If you use the package before the article is formally
published, we would appreciate a citation to the package:

Wenseleers T, Vanderaa C (2026). *GCMSprime: Scalable and Automated
GC–MS Deconvolution, Quantification, and Spectral Library Search in R*.
R package version 0.1.0.9000,
<https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/>.

The [Authors and Citation
page](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/authors.html#citation)
also provides the citation in BibTeX format. Please also cite the
methodological sources linked in the help pages where relevant.

  : Calibrate retention indices from an n-alkane standard

  : Add alkane-calibrated retention indices without a library search

  [`as.data.frame(`*`<GCMSmatches>`*`)`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/reference/librarySearch.md)
  [`print(`*`<GCMSmatches>`*`)`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/reference/librarySearch.md)
  : Identify deconvoluted spectra using retention indices and spectral
  libraries
- [`libraryIonWeights()`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/reference/libraryIonWeights.md)
  : Estimate ion-rarity weights from a spectral library
- [`identifyCompounds()`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/reference/identifyCompounds.md)
  : Annotate recovered GC/MS compounds and export library matches

## Shared tools and package overview

- [`reexports`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/reference/reexports.md)
  [`GIC`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/reference/reexports.md)
  [`gicGap`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/reference/reexports.md)
  [`EBIC`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/reference/reexports.md)
  [`MBIC`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/reference/reexports.md)
  : Objects exported from other packages
- [`GCMSprime`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/reference/GCMSprime-package.md)
  [`GCMSprime-package`](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/reference/GCMSprime-package.md)
  : Scalable and Automated GC–MS Deconvolution, Quantification, and
  Spectral Library Search in R

# Articles

### Tutorials

- [GC/MS deconvolution for single
  samples](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/articles/gcms-deconvolution.md):

  Separate overlapping compounds into log-concave elution profiles and
  full mass spectra.

- [GC/MS deconvolution for multiple
  samples](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/articles/multisample.md):

  Analyze sample directories with alkane calibration, shared spectra and
  sample-specific compound areas.

- [Spectral library
  import](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/articles/spectral-libraries.md):

  Convert Agilent and Shimadzu mass spectral libraries to MSP with
  OpenChrom and import them into GCMSprime.

- [Retention indices and library
  search](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/articles/library-search.md):

### Benchmarks

- [Benchmarks against other
  software](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/articles/benchmarks.md):

  Peak-area accuracy, spectral ion support and elution-profile recovery
  across seven workflows on 16 RI-aware simulated GC–MS chromatograms.

### Algorithm and theory

- [GC/MS deconvolution: mathematical
  basis](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/articles/algorithm.md):

  Grouped L0 selection, alternating PSF estimation, log-concave
  factorization, automatic compound-count selection and noise-aware
  GC/MS analysis.

- [Retention indices and spectral
  identification](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/GCMSprime/articles/identification-theory.md):

  Alkane anchors, onset-based retention calibration, spectral distances,
  ion weighting and scalable matching.
